title: Cipher
directAnswer: Decode a binary string. The encoder takes the original s of length n, writes k right-shifted copies, and XORs the columns, giving an encoded string of length n+k−1 where enc[i] = XOR of s[i−k+1 .. i] (clamped to valid indices). To invert: s[0] = enc[0]; for i ≥ 1, s[i] = enc[i] XOR enc[i−1] XOR (s[i−k] if i ≥ k else 0). The enc[i] XOR enc[i−1] term cancels everything shared between two adjacent windows, leaving just the entering bit s[i] and the leaving bit s[i−k]. Reconstructing each bit naively by re-XORing its window is O(n·k); the difference recurrence is O(n).

remember.pattern: Invert a sliding XOR window via adjacent-window difference
remember.formula:
s[0] = enc[0]
for i in 1..n-1:
    s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1]
    if i >= k: s[i] ^= s[i-k]
# because enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] = s[i] ^ s[i-k]  (window shifted by one)
rules: Encoding is a sliding XOR window of width k: `enc[i] = s[i] ^ s[i-1] ^ … ^ s[i-k+1]`, with out-of-range s treated as 0. Encoded length is `n + k − 1`.
**Adjacent encoded bits differ by exactly the bit entering and the bit leaving the window:** `enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] = s[i] ^ s[i-k]`.
Rearranged, `s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] ^ s[i-k]`, and the `s[i-k]` term only applies once `i ≥ k` (otherwise nothing has left the window yet).
Seed with `s[0] = enc[0]` because the first window contains only `s[0]`.
Use `enc[i-1]`, NOT `s[i-1]`, in the recurrence — the cancellation identity is between consecutive ENCODED bits. Substituting `s[i-1]` is a common but wrong shortcut.
whenToUse: Decode/invert a stream produced by XOR over a sliding window
Telescoping: adjacent prefix/window values cancel to a tiny difference
Reconstruct a sequence from cumulative or windowed XOR sums
Any 'each output mixes the last k inputs by XOR' inversion
antiSignals: The mixing op doesn't cancel on repeats (sum/product window) → need prefix arithmetic, not XOR cancellation
Window width isn't fixed / varies per position → the clean difference identity breaks
You need the encoder, not the decoder → just compute the windowed XOR forward
Encoded length doesn't equal n + k − 1 → re-derive the model before coding
remember.takeaway: Encoding is a width-k sliding XOR window; decoding telescopes it. Two adjacent encoded bits cancel everything except the entering bit s[i] and the leaving bit s[i−k], giving s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i−1] ^ (s[i−k] if i≥k) — one O(n) pass instead of re-summing each window.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can model the encoder as a sliding XOR window and invert it by telescoping adjacent encoded bits, reaching an O(n) recurrence instead of recomputing each bit's window in O(k).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Recomputing each bit's window XOR (O(n·k) and too slow), using s[i-1] instead of enc[i-1] in the recurrence, or mis-handling the i < k boundary where no bit has left the window yet.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Write enc[i] = XOR of the last k bits of s, observe enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] = s[i] ^ s[i-k], and derive s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] ^ (s[i-k] if i≥k) — a single linear pass with O(1) per bit.

problemStatement: A binary string `s` of length `n` is encoded as follows: make `k` copies of `s`, shift the j-th copy right by j positions (j = 0..k−1), align them, and XOR each column. The result is an encoded binary string of length `n + k − 1`. Given the encoded string and the integers `n` and `k`, recover and return the original string `s`.
constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁶ (length of the original string s)
Length of the encoded string is exactly n + k − 1
s and the encoded string contain only the characters '0' and '1'
understanding: Stacking k right-shifted copies of s and XORing columns means column i collects s at positions i, i−1, …, i−k+1 (whichever are in range). So enc[i] is the XOR of the last up-to-k bits of s ending at i — a fixed-width sliding XOR window. Decoding means inverting that window. Because XOR cancels repeats, comparing two neighbouring columns wipes out everything they share and exposes exactly the one bit that entered and the one that left.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What exactly is the relationship between enc[i] and s?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: enc[i] = s[i] XOR s[i−1] XOR … XOR s[i−k+1], where any index < 0 or ≥ n contributes 0. The encoded string has length n + k − 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How do I get s[0]?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The first column contains only s[0] (no earlier bits exist), so s[0] = enc[0].

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why use enc[i] XOR enc[i−1] rather than s[i−1]?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Two adjacent windows overlap in k−1 positions; XORing the two encoded bits cancels that shared overlap, leaving s[i] XOR s[i−k]. That cancellation only happens between the ENCODED values, so it must be enc[i−1], not s[i−1].

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about the boundary when i < k?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Before index k, the window hasn't dropped any bit yet, so there is no s[i−k] term — only enc[i] XOR enc[i−1] (plus s[0] = enc[0] as the seed).

examples.explanation: The classic example: four shifted copies of "1001010" XORed column-wise produce "1110100110"; the recurrence reconstructs "1001010".
With k = 1 the window is a single bit, so enc == s. Decoding returns the input unchanged.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Recompute Each Bit's Window
approaches.whenToMention: Say this first: it inverts the encoder definition literally before you find the telescoping shortcut.
hints: From enc[i] = s[i] XOR (the previous up-to-k−1 already-decoded bits), solve for s[i].
s[0] = enc[0]. For i ≥ 1, s[i] = enc[i] XOR (s[i−1] XOR … XOR s[i−k+1]), clamping the lower index at 0.
Recomputing that inner XOR for every i costs up to k work each → O(n·k). Correct, but too slow when n and k are both 10⁶.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each of the n bits recomputes a window of up to k−1 previously-decoded bits → O(n·k) in the worst case (~10¹² when both are 10⁶), which is far too slow.
approaches.explanation:
Invert the encoder directly, one bit at a time.

**The inversion.** By definition `enc[i] = s[i] ^ s[i-1] ^ … ^ s[i-k+1]`. Everything in that XOR except `s[i]` has already been decoded by the time we reach position `i`. So `s[i] = enc[i] ^ (s[i-1] ^ … ^ s[i-k+1])`, treating indices below 0 as absent. Seed with `s[0] = enc[0]` since the first window holds only `s[0]`.

**How the loop runs.** For each `i`, gather the XOR of the previously decoded bits in the window `[max(0, i-k+1), i-1]`, then XOR with `enc[i]` to recover `s[i]`.

**Why it's correct but slow.** It exactly reverses the encoding, so it always produces the right `s`. But recomputing the window XOR from scratch at every position does up to `k-1` XORs per bit, giving `O(n·k)`. With both `n` and `k` up to `10⁶`, that's `~10¹²` operations — hopeless. The fix is to avoid recomputing the overlap, which is what the telescoping recurrence does.
approaches.insight: Two consecutive windows share k−1 bits. Recomputing that shared region every step is the wasted work; the optimal approach cancels it with a single XOR of adjacent encoded bits.

diagrams.title: Recomputing each window
diagrams.caption: Every bit re-XORs up to k−1 prior bits — the overlap the optimal solution skips.

pitfalls: Forgetting to clamp the window's lower index at 0 for the first k−1 positions.
Recomputing the full window each step — the O(n·k) blowup that times out at 10⁶.
Off-by-one on the window: it covers s[i−k+1 .. i−1] of already-decoded bits, not including i.

approaches.name: Telescoping Recurrence — Adjacent-Window Difference (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Say 'XOR two adjacent encoded bits to cancel the overlap: s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] ^ (s[i-k] if i≥k)'.
hints: Write out enc[i] and enc[i−1] as XORs of overlapping windows. What survives when you XOR them together?
The two windows share s[i−1 .. i−k+1]; those cancel, leaving enc[i] ^ enc[i−1] = s[i] ^ s[i−k].
So s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i−1] ^ s[i−k], with the s[i−k] term only when i ≥ k. Seed s[0] = enc[0]. One pass, O(1) per bit.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single left-to-right pass computing each s[i] from two encoded bits and one earlier decoded bit — O(1) per position, O(n) total, with O(n) space for the output.
approaches.explanation:
Cancel the window overlap instead of recomputing it.

**The telescoping identity.** The window for position `i` is `s[i] ^ s[i-1] ^ … ^ s[i-k+1]`; for position `i-1` it is `s[i-1] ^ s[i-2] ^ … ^ s[i-k]`. These two windows overlap in the k−1 positions `i-1 … i-k+1`. XORing the two encoded bits cancels that shared block:

`enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] = s[i] ^ s[i-k]`

because `s[i]` is in the first window but not the second (it just entered), and `s[i-k]` is in the second but not the first (it just left). Everything in between appears in both and cancels.

**Solve for s[i].** Rearranging, `s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] ^ s[i-k]`. The leaving bit `s[i-k]` only exists once `i ≥ k`; before that nothing has dropped out of the window, so the term is omitted. The seed is `s[0] = enc[0]` (first window = just s[0]).

**Why it must be enc[i-1], not s[i-1].** The cancellation is an algebraic identity between the two ENCODED values. Substituting `s[i-1]` for `enc[i-1]` breaks it and produces wrong bits from the third position onward — a tempting but incorrect shortcut.

**Why it's fast.** Each bit costs two XORs and one array read: O(1). One left-to-right pass decodes the whole string in O(n), which is essential at n, k up to 10⁶.
approaches.insight: Decoding a sliding XOR window telescopes: neighbouring encoded bits cancel their shared overlap, exposing only the bit that entered (s[i]) and the bit that left (s[i−k]). That single observation turns an O(n·k) re-summation into an O(n) recurrence.

edgeCases.behavior: Window width 1 → enc == s. The recurrence gives s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] ^ s[i-1] = enc[i], returning the input unchanged.
Only s[0] = enc[0]; the loop never runs.

pitfalls: Using s[i-1] instead of enc[i-1] — breaks the cancellation identity from i = 2 onward.
Applying the s[i-k] term when i < k (no bit has left yet) and corrupting the early bits.
Reading enc[i-1] off the partially built s array rather than the original encoded string.

commonMistakes: Recomputing each bit's window XOR → O(n·k) and a timeout at n, k = 10⁶.
Substituting s[i-1] for enc[i-1] in the recurrence, which is algebraically wrong.
Mishandling the i < k boundary where no bit has yet left the window.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using s[i-1] instead of enc[i-1]
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The telescoping identity enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] = s[i] ^ s[i-k] holds for the ENCODED values. Swapping in the decoded s[i-1] breaks the cancellation and yields wrong bits from position 2 on.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
bit = int(encoded[i]) ^ s[i - 1]      # wrong: should be enc[i-1]
if i >= k: bit ^= s[i - k]
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
bit = int(encoded[i]) ^ int(encoded[i - 1])
if i >= k: bit ^= s[i - k]

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Applying the leaving term too early
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Before index k, the window hasn't dropped any bit, so there is no s[i-k] to remove. Adding it (or indexing s[i-k] with a negative index) corrupts the first bits.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int bit = cur ^ (encoded.charAt(i - 1) - '0');
bit ^= (s[i - k] - '0');             // i-k can be negative when i < k
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int bit = cur ^ (encoded.charAt(i - 1) - '0');
if (i >= k) bit ^= (s[i - k] - '0');

commonMistakesDetailed.title: O(n·k) window recomputation
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Re-XORing up to k−1 prior bits for every position is correct but quadratic-ish; at n, k = 10⁶ it's ~10¹² ops and times out. Telescope instead.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
for i in range(1, n):
    window = 0
    for j in range(max(0, i - k + 1), i):   # O(k) each
        window ^= s[j]
    s[i] = int(encoded[i]) ^ window
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
for i in range(1, n):
    bit = int(encoded[i]) ^ int(encoded[i - 1])
    if i >= k: bit ^= s[i - k]
    s[i] = bit

patternNote: Invert a sliding XOR window by telescoping. When each output XORs a fixed window of inputs, neighbouring outputs cancel their overlap, exposing only the entering and leaving terms: s[i] = enc[i] ^ enc[i-1] ^ s[i-k]. This converts an O(n·k) reconstruction into an O(n) recurrence — the XOR analogue of prefix-sum differencing.
